phase1.intro:
A method is a reusable block of code you can call by name instead of retyping it every time you need it.

What should we open first?

topics.buttonText: What does a method actually look like?
dialogue: The shape is always the same: `static returnType name(parameters) { body }`. The return type tells Java what kind of value comes back out — or `void`, if nothing comes back at all.
Parameters are the values you hand IN when you call it.

stickyNote.definition: static returnType name(parameters) { body } — returnType is void if nothing is returned; parameters are the values passed in.

topics.buttonText: Can two methods share the same name?
dialogue: [[term:Method overloading]] is writing several methods with the same name but different parameter lists — Java tells them apart by looking at what you actually passed in, not by the name alone.
`add(int a, int b)` and `add(int a, int b, int c)` can both exist side by side, and Java picks the right one based on how many arguments you give it.

stickyNote.definition: Multiple methods sharing a name but differing in parameter list. Java picks the right one based on the arguments passed.

topics.buttonText: Why bother breaking code into methods at all?
dialogue: [[key:Methods exist for three real reasons]]: you write the logic once instead of copy-pasting it everywhere, you break a big problem into smaller understandable pieces, and a well-named method reads almost like plain English at the call site.
`factorial(5)` tells you exactly what's happening without needing to look inside it.

stickyNote.flavor: 📖 write once, break it down, read like English
stickyNote.definition: Methods avoid repeated code, break big problems into pieces, and make call sites self-explanatory — e.g. factorial(5).

phase1.openingDialogue: A method is a reusable, callable block of code — same shape every time, and overloadable by parameter list. 🧰

phase2.errorMessage:
MethodsExample.java:7: error: invalid method declaration; return type required
    static add(int a, int b) {
           ^
1 error
phase2.explanation:
[[warn:Every method needs an explicit return type — even one that returns nothing]]. `void` isn't optional decoration, it's a required part of the declaration.

`static add(int a, int b)` is missing that piece entirely — Java has no idea whether this method is supposed to hand back an int, a double, nothing at all, or something else. [[key:The fix is just naming what actually comes back]]: `static int add(int a, int b)`, since this one returns a sum.

phase3.openingDialogue: Time to create your own reusable blocks — methods! 🛠️

mcq.question:
What lets Java tell apart two methods that share the exact same name?

A) Their return type alone
B) Their parameter list (number/types of parameters)
C) The order they're written in the file
D) Java doesn't allow same-named methods at all

phase4.selfChallenge:
Write a program with these methods:
1. multiply(int a, int b) — returns a * b
2. multiply(int a, int b, int c) — returns a * b * c (overloaded)
3. printMessage(String msg) — prints "=== [msg] ==="

Call all three methods from main.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: overloading and overriding sound similar but Java resolves them completely differently under the hood — which overloaded method gets called is decided at compile time, based on the argument types you write. We'll hit the runtime version of this idea — overriding — once we get into inheritance, and the distinction actually matters a lot there.
phase5.openingDialogue: One more thing before you go build your own blocks~
